Denise, I found your note about Colombia this morning, under about forty others. I nearly missed it. Tell me on this call what you need, and then we will fix the email.
Your sign-off on two clauses. By Thursday we will have closed the renewal, so Wednesday evening is the real deadline, not Thursday.
Then that sentence should have been your subject line. Yours says Colombia, update. What was I supposed to do with an update?
Nothing, which is why it sat there. I wrote it the way I would write it in Portuguese. Context first, the request at the end, and a paragraph of courtesy before either of them.
Put the ask at the top and the date next to it. Anything I open after nine at night, I read two lines of. That is not attitude, Denise. That is bandwidth.

Understood. The thread below the ask has the two clauses that changed, and the rest is the boilerplate we have used since March. I have also looped in Mexico, because the same wording will be going to them in April.
Good, and put exactly that in writing, not only on this call. I want a written trail and so do you. What is your turnaround if I come back with questions on Wednesday?
Same day. I will acknowledge within the hour even if the answer takes until the evening. And if I have not heard from you by Wednesday evening, I will chase once and then proceed as drafted.
That last sentence is the whole email. Lead with it next time and I will be answering you before lunch.
If I have not heard from you by Wednesday evening, I will chase once and then proceed as drafted.

I get somewhere between two and three hundred messages a day, and I want to be honest with you about what I actually read. The subject line and the first two lines. That is the whole decision. Everything after that gets read only if those two lines have earned it. So the subject line has to carry the ask and the date, not the topic. Colombia update tells me nothing and it will sit there for a week. Colombia renewal, decision needed by Thursday tells me what you want and when, and I can act on it between two meetings. If I cannot see the ask straight away, the message goes into the pile I will get to on Sunday, and Sunday is where good work goes to die. One more rule, and people always resist it. If you have three things to ask me, send three emails with one ask in each. You will get three answers. Send one email with three asks and you will get an answer to the first one.

For a long time I opened every English email with two or three lines of warmth, the way I would in my own language. I hope this message finds you well. Apologies for the extra work. Thank you so much in advance. I stopped, and not because anybody was rude about it. I stopped because I finally understood how those lines were landing. They were reading as hesitation, and hesitation from a director reads as doubt about her own request. Here is what took me years to accept. Directness does not sound childish. The pile of apologies around the ask is what sounds childish. So the warm sentence still exists in my emails, but it lives at the end now, and it is one sentence instead of a paragraph. And I never apologise for a deadline. A deadline is a fact of the business, not a favour I am asking for. I state it, and I say what happens if it moves.

By Thursday we will have closed the Colombian renewal, and I need your sign-off on the wording before then. The thread below has the two clauses that changed, and the rest is the boilerplate we have used since March. I have looped in Mexico, because the same wording will be going to them in April. If I have not heard from you by Wednesday evening, I will chase once and then proceed as drafted.
